hook: Global ocean temperature records have been broken for 165 days in a row.

sections.voiceover: Global ocean temperature records have been broken for 165 days in a row.
sections.visual_cue: A digital counter rapidly ticking up to 165 over a satellite view of the ocean.
sections.sfx_cue: Rapid ticking sound increasing in intensity.
b_roll: Satellite view of global ocean surface currents

sections.voiceover: In October 2026, the National Centers for Environmental Information confirmed sea surface temperatures set an all-time high. How hot is the water?
sections.visual_cue: A heat map showing rising temperatures across the Pacific ocean region.
b_roll: NOAA ocean temperature heatmap for October 2026

sections.voiceover: The NOAA Climate Prediction Center reports the Pacific Ocean's Niño3.4 temperature anomaly hit 2.2 degrees Celsius.
sections.visual_cue: Close up of the Niño3.4 region on a Pacific map with the 2.2 degree figure highlighted.
b_roll: Animated map of the Niño3.4 region

sections.voiceover: Copernicus reports this year is virtually certain to surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
sections.visual_cue: A line graph showing the 5.3 degree anomaly spike.
b_roll: Copernicus climate data chart showing 1.5 degree threshold

sections.voiceover: The world has seen 165 days of record-shattering ocean heat.
sections.visual_cue: Wide shot of the Earth from space with a glowing ocean texture.
b_roll: Earth from space showing ocean surface
